title: Partial derivatives
description: Read how a function of several variables changes when you move in just one direction.
sourceFiles: CRAMMED demonstration notes — not course material

topics.title: Change one variable at a time

sections.title: Hold the others steady
sections.body: For a function of several variables, a partial derivative measures change with respect to one variable while the other variables are held constant.

sections.title: Notation
sections.body:
For z = f(x, y):
∂f/∂x  or  fₓ
∂f/∂y  or  fᵧ

sections.title: Change one input
sections.body: For f(x, y) = x²y + 3y, hold y fixed: fₓ = 2xy. At (3, 2), the rate of change in the x direction is 12; changing y is a separate question.

sections.title: Easy mix-up
sections.body: When differentiating with respect to x, terms containing only y are constants, but they do not disappear unless their derivative with respect to x is zero.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Differentiate with respect to the named variable; treat all the other variables as constants.

sections.title: Differentiate again
sections.body: A second partial derivative differentiates a first partial derivative once more. You can differentiate twice with respect to the same variable or use two different variables.

sections.title: Follow the order
sections.body: For f(x, y) = x²y, first find fₓ = 2xy. Now differentiate that result with respect to y: fₓᵧ = 2x. At x = 3, this mixed partial is 6.

sections.title: Mixed partials
sections.body: A mixed partial derivative differentiates with respect to more than one variable, in a specified order.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Read subscripts as instructions. For fₓᵧ, find fₓ first, then differentiate that result with respect to y.

sections.title: A vector of partial derivatives
sections.body: For a differentiable scalar-valued function, the gradient collects its first partial derivatives into a vector. It points in the direction of greatest local increase.

sections.title: A height map
sections.body: Treat f(x, y) = x² + y² as the height of a bowl. At (3, 4), ∇f = ⟨6, 8⟩ points toward the steepest climb. The direction—not just the height—is what the gradient adds.

sections.title: Keep the distinction
sections.body: The function value is a scalar. Its gradient is a vector made from its partial derivatives.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Build the gradient from first partial derivatives. For a scalar field, it points toward greatest increase.

questions.prompt: For f(x, y) = x²y + 3y, what is ∂f/∂x?
questions.explanation: Treat y as a constant and differentiate x²y + 3y with respect to x, giving 2xy.

questions.prompt: For f(x, y) = x²y, what is fₓᵧ?
questions.explanation: First fₓ = 2xy; differentiating that with respect to y gives 2x.

questions.prompt: What kind of quantity is the gradient of a scalar-valued function?
questions.explanation: The gradient collects the first partial derivatives into a vector.

questions.prompt: When calculating ∂f/∂y, what do you do with x?
options: Differentiate with respect to x too
questions.explanation: In a partial derivative with respect to y, the other variables are held constant.
